claim: Kir4.1 is broadly expressed by CNS glia.
source: The inwardly rectifying K+ channel Kir4.1 is broadly expressed by CNS glia and deficits in Kir4.1 lead to seizures and myelin vacuolization.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about Kir4.1 expression.

claim: Deficits in Kir4.1 lead to seizures and myelin vacuolization.
source: The inwardly rectifying K+ channel Kir4.1 is broadly expressed by CNS glia and deficits in Kir4.1 lead to seizures and myelin vacuolization.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the consequences of Kir4.1 deficits.

claim: Selective deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocyte progenitors did not impair their development.
source: Here, we show that selective deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocyte progenitors (OPCs) or mature oligodendrocytes did not impair their development or disrupt the structure of myelin.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: Selective deletion of Kir4.1 from mature oligodendrocytes did not disrupt the structure of myelin.
source: Here, we show that selective deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocyte progenitors (OPCs) or mature oligodendrocytes did not impair their development or disrupt the structure of myelin.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: Mice lacking oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 channels exhibited slower clearance of extracellular K+ in white matter.
source: However, mice lacking oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 channels exhibited profound functional impairments, including slower clearance of extracellular K+ and delayed recovery of axons from repetitive stimulation in white matter, as well as spontaneous seizures, a lower seizure threshold, and activity-dependent motor deficits.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental measurements.

claim: Mice lacking oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 channels exhibited delayed recovery of axons from repetitive stimulation in white matter.
source: However, mice lacking oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 channels exhibited profound functional impairments, including slower clearance of extracellular K+ and delayed recovery of axons from repetitive stimulation in white matter, as well as spontaneous seizures, a lower seizure threshold, and activity-dependent motor deficits.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental measurements.

claim: Mice lacking oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 channels exhibited spontaneous seizures.
source: However, mice lacking oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 channels exhibited profound functional impairments, including slower clearance of extracellular K+ and delayed recovery of axons from repetitive stimulation in white matter, as well as spontaneous seizures, a lower seizure threshold, and activity-dependent motor deficits.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: Mice lacking oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 channels exhibited a lower seizure threshold.
source: However, mice lacking oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 channels exhibited profound functional impairments, including slower clearance of extracellular K+ and delayed recovery of axons from repetitive stimulation in white matter, as well as spontaneous seizures, a lower seizure threshold, and activity-dependent motor deficits.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental measurements.

claim: Mice lacking oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 channels exhibited activity-dependent motor deficits.
source: However, mice lacking oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 channels exhibited profound functional impairments, including slower clearance of extracellular K+ and delayed recovery of axons from repetitive stimulation in white matter, as well as spontaneous seizures, a lower seizure threshold, and activity-dependent motor deficits.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on behavioral testing.

claim: Kir4.1 channels in oligodendrocytes play an important role in extracellular K+ homeostasis in white matter.
source: These results indicate that Kir4.1 channels in oligodendrocytes play an important role in extracellular K+ homeostasis in white matter, and that selective loss of this channel from oligodendrocytes is sufficient to impair K+ clearance and promote seizures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Selective loss of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes is sufficient to impair K+ clearance and promote seizures.
source: These results indicate that Kir4.1 channels in oligodendrocytes play an important role in extracellular K+ homeostasis in white matter, and that selective loss of this channel from oligodendrocytes is sufficient to impair K+ clearance and promote seizures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Action potentials lead to increases in extracellular K+ that can impair membrane repolarization, induce tonic firing and trigger seizures if left unchecked.
source: Action potentials lead to increases in extracellular K+ that if left unchecked can impair membrane repolarization, induce tonic firing and trigger seizures.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the consequences of extracellular K+ accumulation.

claim: The redistribution of extracellular K+ following neuronal activity is mediated through diffusion and uptake into cells (K+ buffering).
source: The redistribution of extracellular K+ following neuronal activity is mediated through diffusion and uptake into cells (K+ buffering), particularly glial cells which maintain a high resting conductance to K+ and a highly negative resting potential (Kofuji and Newman, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Glial cells maintain a high resting conductance to K+ and a highly negative resting potential.
source: The redistribution of extracellular K+ following neuronal activity is mediated through diffusion and uptake into cells (K+ buffering), particularly glial cells which maintain a high resting conductance to K+ and a highly negative resting potential (Kofuji and Newman, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Astrocytes have been shown to participate in K+ buffering in gray matter.
source: In gray matter, astrocytes have been shown to participate in K+ buffering, but much less is known about the mechanisms that enable K+ clearance in white matter, where astrocyte access to axons is limited to nodes of Ranvier and the majority of axonal K+ channels are located beneath the myelin sheath (Rash et al., 2016; Wang et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Astrocyte access to axons in white matter is limited to nodes of Ranvier.
source: In gray matter, astrocytes have been shown to participate in K+ buffering, but much less is known about the mechanisms that enable K+ clearance in white matter, where astrocyte access to axons is limited to nodes of Ranvier and the majority of axonal K+ channels are located beneath the myelin sheath (Rash et al., 2016; Wang et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The majority of axonal K+ channels are located beneath the myelin sheath.
source: In gray matter, astrocytes have been shown to participate in K+ buffering, but much less is known about the mechanisms that enable K+ clearance in white matter, where astrocyte access to axons is limited to nodes of Ranvier and the majority of axonal K+ channels are located beneath the myelin sheath (Rash et al., 2016; Wang et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Oligodendrocytes have extended contact with axons and exhibit a high resting conductance to K+.
source: Oligodendrocytes have extended contact with axons and exhibit a high resting conductance to K+, but their contribution to K+ clearance in white matter and the impact of this K+ redistribution on neuronal activity has not been determined.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about oligodendrocyte properties.

claim: Kir4.1 is the most abundant K+ channel expressed by astrocytes and oligodendroglia.
source: Kir4.1 is the most abundant K+ channel expressed by astrocytes and oligodendroglia (Zhang et al., 2014) and has been shown to help establish their resting membrane potential (Djukic et al., 2007; Neusch et al., 2006) and to redistribute extracellular K+ in gray matter following neuronal activity (Chever et al., 2010; Haj-Yasein et al., 2011; Neusch et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Kir4.1 helps establish the resting membrane potential of astrocytes and oligodendroglia.
source: Kir4.1 is the most abundant K+ channel expressed by astrocytes and oligodendroglia (Zhang et al., 2014) and has been shown to help establish their resting membrane potential (Djukic et al., 2007; Neusch et al., 2006) and to redistribute extracellular K+ in gray matter following neuronal activity (Chever et al., 2010; Haj-Yasein et al., 2011; Neusch et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Kir4.1 redistributes extracellular K+ in gray matter following neuronal activity.
source: Kir4.1 is the most abundant K+ channel expressed by astrocytes and oligodendroglia (Zhang et al., 2014) and has been shown to help establish their resting membrane potential (Djukic et al., 2007; Neusch et al., 2006) and to redistribute extracellular K+ in gray matter following neuronal activity (Chever et al., 2010; Haj-Yasein et al., 2011; Neusch et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Kir4.1 knockout mice exhibit ataxia, seizures, deafness, widespread myelin pathology, and early death.
source: The importance of Kir4.1 in K+ homeostasis is underscored by the severe neurological phenotype of Kir4.1 knockout mice, which exhibit ataxia, seizures, deafness, widespread myelin pathology, and early death (Djukic et al., 2007; Neusch et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Many features of Kir4.1 knockout mice are observed in human patients with SeSAME/EAST syndrome.
source: Many of these features are also observed in human patients with SeSAME/EAST syndrome, a rare genetic disease caused by loss-of-function mutations in Kir4.1 (Bockenhauer et al., 2009; Scholl et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: SeSAME/EAST syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in Kir4.1.
source: Many of these features are also observed in human patients with SeSAME/EAST syndrome, a rare genetic disease caused by loss-of-function mutations in Kir4.1 (Bockenhauer et al., 2009; Scholl et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Polymorphisms in the Kir4.1 gene are associated with idiopathic epilepsy.
source: Polymorphisms in the Kir4.1 gene are associated with idiopathic epilepsy (Buono et al., 2004; Heuser et al., 2010; Lenzen et al., 2005) and autism spectrum disorder with seizures (Sicca et al., 2011; 2016), futher supporting a close functional link between Kir4.1 dysfunction and neuronal hyperexcitability.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Polymorphisms in the Kir4.1 gene are associated with autism spectrum disorder with seizures.
source: Polymorphisms in the Kir4.1 gene are associated with idiopathic epilepsy (Buono et al., 2004; Heuser et al., 2010; Lenzen et al., 2005) and autism spectrum disorder with seizures (Sicca et al., 2011; 2016), futher supporting a close functional link between Kir4.1 dysfunction and neuronal hyperexcitability.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Kir4.1 expression levels are reduced in a vast array of CNS pathologies.
source: Kir4.1 expression levels are reduced in a vast array of CNS pathologies (for review, see Nwaobi et al., 2016), and restoration of astrocyte Kir4.1 levels in the striatum of Huntington's disease model mice enhanced neuronal suvival and ameliorated motor deficits (Tong et al., 2014), suggesting that impaired K+ buffering may contribute to both genetic and aquired neurological disease.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Restoration of astrocyte Kir4.1 levels in the striatum of Huntington's disease model mice enhanced neuronal survival and ameliorated motor deficits.
source: Kir4.1 expression levels are reduced in a vast array of CNS pathologies (for review, see Nwaobi et al., 2016), and restoration of astrocyte Kir4.1 levels in the striatum of Huntington's disease model mice enhanced neuronal suvival and ameliorated motor deficits (Tong et al., 2014), suggesting that impaired K+ buffering may contribute to both genetic and aquired neurological disease.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) express Kir4.1.
source: Although the pathological sequelae arising from Kir4.1 dysfunction are commonly attributed to astrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) and mature oligodendrocytes have also been shown to express Kir4.1, by immunohistochemistry (Kalsi et al., 2004; Poopalasundaram et al., 2000), reporter gene expression (Tang et al., 2009), RNA-Seq (Tasic et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2014) and recordings of Kir-mediated currents (Battefeld et al., 2016; Maldonado et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Mature oligodendrocytes express Kir4.1.
source: Although the pathological sequelae arising from Kir4.1 dysfunction are commonly attributed to astrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) and mature oligodendrocytes have also been shown to express Kir4.1, by immunohistochemistry (Kalsi et al., 2004; Poopalasundaram et al., 2000), reporter gene expression (Tang et al., 2009), RNA-Seq (Tasic et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2014) and recordings of Kir-mediated currents (Battefeld et al., 2016; Maldonado et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: OPCs that lack Kir4.1 fail to fully mature into oligodendrocytes in vitro.
source: OPCs that lack Kir4.1 fail to fully mature into oligodendrocytes in vitro (Neusch et al., 2001), and white matter tracts in glial-specific Kir4.1 knockout mice exhibit extensive vacuolization (Djukic et al., 2007), suggesting that this K+ channel performs diverse roles in oligodendroglia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: White matter tracts in glial-specific Kir4.1 knockout mice exhibit extensive vacuolization.
source: OPCs that lack Kir4.1 fail to fully mature into oligodendrocytes in vitro (Neusch et al., 2001), and white matter tracts in glial-specific Kir4.1 knockout mice exhibit extensive vacuolization (Djukic et al., 2007), suggesting that this K+ channel performs diverse roles in oligodendroglia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Selective depolarization of oligodendrocytes in white matter alters the conduction speed of action potentials.
source: Functional studies indicate that selective depolarization of oligodendrocytes in white matter alters the conduction speed of action potentials, an effect that is abolished by application of a Kir channel blocker (Yamazaki et al., 2007; 2014), suggesting that oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 channels can shape neuronal activity on a rapid time scale.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The effect of oligodendrocyte depolarization on action potential conduction speed is abolished by application of a Kir channel blocker.
source: Functional studies indicate that selective depolarization of oligodendrocytes in white matter alters the conduction speed of action potentials, an effect that is abolished by application of a Kir channel blocker (Yamazaki et al., 2007; 2014), suggesting that oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 channels can shape neuronal activity on a rapid time scale.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: nKir4.1cKO mice exhibited retarded growth, ataxia, tremor, and early mortality, with most mice dying by postnatal day 25.
source: These nervous-system-specific Kir4.1 conditional knockout mice (termed nKir4.1cKO) exhibited retarded growth, ataxia, tremor, and early mortality, with most mice dying by postnatal day (P) 25 (Figure 1A–B; Figure 1—video 1), similar to the phenotype of Kir4.1 global knockout and glia-specific Kir4.1 knockout mice (Djukic et al., 2007; Neusch et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental observations.

claim: Kir4.1 immunoreactivity was no longer observed in the brains of nKir4.1cKO mice.
source: Kir4.1 immunoreactivity was no longer observed in the brains of these mice (Figure 1C), demonstrating effective deletion of this channel from the CNS.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: nKir4.1cKO mice exhibited widespread vacuolization of myelin.
source: Immunostaining for myelin basic protein (MBP) revealed dense myelinated tracts in the corpus callosum and striatum, indicating that oligodendrocytes were formed; however, these regions exhibited widespread vacuolization of myelin, with swellings visible along most internodes (Figure 1D–F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: The density of oligodendrocytes in nKir4.1cKO mice at P24 was comparable to control mice.
source: Despite these striking morphological changes, the density of oligodendrocytes in nKir4.1cKO mice at P24, measured by immunostaining for the oligodendrocyte protein aspartoacylase (ASPA), was comparable to control mice (Nes-Cre;Kcnj10fl/+) (Figure 1G,H), indicating that oligodendrocytes are generated and mature in the absence of Kir4.1.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on quantification of immunostaining data shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: OPC density was unchanged in nKir4.1cKO mice.
source: This analysis revealed that OPC density was unchanged (Figure 1J) in nKir4.1cKO mice, and their proliferation was reduced, rather than increased (Figure 1K), suggesting that oligodendrocyte turnover is not increased.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on quantification of immunostaining data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: OPC proliferation was reduced in nKir4.1cKO mice.
source: This analysis revealed that OPC density was unchanged (Figure 1J) in nKir4.1cKO mice, and their proliferation was reduced, rather than increased (Figure 1K), suggesting that oligodendrocyte turnover is not increased.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on quantification of Ki67 immunostaining data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Oligodendrocytes in the corpus callosum of nKir4.1cKO mice at P21 were significantly depolarized compared to controls.
source: EGFP+ oligodendrocytes in the corpus callosum of these mice at P21 were significantly depolarized compared to controls (Nes-Cre;Mobp-EGFP) (control: –77 ± 2 mV, n = 5; cKO: –31 ± 1 mV, n = 4; p=7.6 × 10–7) (Figure 1M), but maintained the membrane resistance and linear current-voltage response characteristic of WT oligodendrocytes (Figure 1M,N).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1M.

claim: Oligodendrocytes in nKir4.1cKO mice maintained the membrane resistance characteristic of WT oligodendrocytes.
source: EGFP+ oligodendrocytes in the corpus callosum of these mice at P21 were significantly depolarized compared to controls (Nes-Cre;Mobp-EGFP) (control: –77 ± 2 mV, n = 5; cKO: –31 ± 1 mV, n = 4; p=7.6 × 10–7) (Figure 1M), but maintained the membrane resistance and linear current-voltage response characteristic of WT oligodendrocytes (Figure 1M,N).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1M.

claim: Deletion of Kir4.1 from the CNS leads to profound changes in the structure of myelin but does not impair oligodendrocyte maturation or accelerate their degeneration during development.
source: Together these results indicate that deletion of Kir4.1 from the CNS leads to profound changes in the structure of myelin and depolarization of oligodendrocytes but does not impair their maturation or accelerate their degeneration during development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Kir4.1 is the most abundant K+ channel expressed by OPCs.
source: Kir4.1 is the most abundant K+ channel expressed by OPCs (Larson et al., 2016), and upregulation of these channels, as assessed by the appearance of Ba2+-sensitive Kir currents, correlates with development of a more negative OPC membrane potential and acquisition of a linear I-V curve profile over the course of postnatal development (Maldonado et al., 2013), suggesting that Kir4.1 plays a key role in establishing the membrane properties of these progenitors.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Upregulation of Kir4.1 channels correlates with development of a more negative OPC membrane potential and acquisition of a linear I-V curve profile over the course of postnatal development.
source: Kir4.1 is the most abundant K+ channel expressed by OPCs (Larson et al., 2016), and upregulation of these channels, as assessed by the appearance of Ba2+-sensitive Kir currents, correlates with development of a more negative OPC membrane potential and acquisition of a linear I-V curve profile over the course of postnatal development (Maldonado et al., 2013), suggesting that Kir4.1 plays a key role in establishing the membrane properties of these progenitors.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The majority of OPCs (76%) in pKir4.1cKO mice exhibited greatly reduced inward currents in response to hyperpolarization.
source: In contrast, the majority of OPCs (49/65, 76%) in pKir4.1cKO mice exhibited greatly reduced inward currents in response to hyperpolarization, and BaCl2 (100 µM) did not alter their I-V relationship, indicating that Kir4.1 was no longer expressed (Figure 2E,G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2E,G.

claim: OPCs in both gray and white matter that lacked Kir4.1 were ~20 mV more depolarized than control OPCs.
source: OPCs in both gray and white matter that lacked Kir4.1 were ~20 mV more depolarized and exhibited a ~ 10 fold higher membrane resistance (measured at –80 mV with a 10 mV depolarization step) than control OPCs (Figure 2H–I; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2H-I.

claim: OPCs that lacked Kir4.1 exhibited a ~10 fold higher membrane resistance than control OPCs.
source: OPCs in both gray and white matter that lacked Kir4.1 were ~20 mV more depolarized and exhibited a ~ 10 fold higher membrane resistance (measured at –80 mV with a 10 mV depolarization step) than control OPCs (Figure 2H–I; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2H-I.

claim: Kir4.1 channels dominate the resting conductance of OPCs and force these progenitors to adopt a more hyperpolarized membrane potential.
source: These results indicate that Kir4.1 channels dominate the resting conductance of OPCs and force these progenitors to adopt a more hyperpolarized membrane potential.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: There was no change in the density of OPCs between control and pKir4.1cKO mice.
source: If OPC proliferation or survival is impaired, a decrease in the relative proportion of EYFP+ OPCs is expected; however, there was no change in the density of OPCs or the proportion of EYFP+ OPCs between control and pKir4.1cKO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on quantification of immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no change in the proportion of EYFP+ OPCs between control and pKir4.1cKO mice.
source: If OPC proliferation or survival is impaired, a decrease in the relative proportion of EYFP+ OPCs is expected; however, there was no change in the density of OPCs or the proportion of EYFP+ OPCs between control and pKir4.1cKO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on quantification of immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: No differences in OPC proliferation were observed between EYFP+ and EYFP– populations in either hippocampus or corpus callosum.
source: Although the proportion of BrdU+ OPCs varied by region, from ~45% in hippocampus to ~60% in corpus callosum, no differences were observed between EYFP+ and EYFP– populations in either region (Figure 3B–E; Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–C), indicating comparable rates of proliferation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on quantification of BrdU incorporation shown in Figure 3B-E.

claim: No significant differences in OPC differentiation were observed between control and Kir4.1-deleted OPCs.
source: At this time point, EYFP+ cells consisted of ~75% PDGFRα+ OPCs and ~15% CC1+ oligodendrocytes in the hippocampus, and ~45% OPCs and ~40% oligodendrocytes in the corpus callosum, with no significant differences observed between control and Kir4.1-deleted OPCs (Figure 3F–H; Figure 3—figure supplement 3D–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on quantification of immunostaining data shown in Figure 3F-H.

claim: Depolarization and increased membrane resistance induced by Kir4.1 deletion did not alter OPC proliferation or differentiation into oligodendrocytes.
source: Thus, although OPCs lacking Kir4.1 exhibited markedly higher membrane resistance and more depolarized membrane potential, remarkably, these changes did not alter their proliferation or differentiation into oligodendrocytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Oligodendrocytes in mixed glial cultures from Kcnj10−/− mice are significantly depolarized and fail to mature fully.
source: Oligodendrocytes in mixed glial cultures from Kcnj10−/− mice are significantly depolarized and fail to mature fully (Neusch et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Selective deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes did not alter their membrane properties.
source: However, selective deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes did not alter their membrane properties, the structure of myelin (Figure 4), or the baseline conduction velocity of action potentials in white matter (Figure 4D; Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: Selective deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes did not alter the structure of myelin.
source: However, selective deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes did not alter their membrane properties, the structure of myelin (Figure 4), or the baseline conduction velocity of action potentials in white matter (Figure 4D; Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on immunostaining and TEM data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Selective deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes did not alter the baseline conduction velocity of action potentials in white matter.
source: However, selective deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes did not alter their membrane properties, the structure of myelin (Figure 4), or the baseline conduction velocity of action potentials in white matter (Figure 4D; Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4D and Figure 7B-C.

claim: Oligodendrocytes express a variety of K+ leak channels that may compensate for the loss of Kir4.1, including K2P channels and the inward-rectifying channel Kir2.1.
source: Oligodendrocytes express a variety of K+ leak channels that may compensate for the loss of Kir4.1, including K2P channels and the inward-rectifying channel Kir2.1 (Gipson and Bordey, 2002; Hawkins and Butt, 2013; Pérez-Samartín et al., 2017; Stonehouse et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Astrocytes in Kcnj10−/− mice are severely depolarized.
source: Astrocytes in Kcnj10−/− mice are also severely depolarized, and their ability to remove extracellular K+ is impaired (Djukic et al., 2007), consistent with their high expression of this channel.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The ability of astrocytes to remove extracellular K+ is impaired in Kcnj10−/− mice.
source: Astrocytes in Kcnj10−/− mice are also severely depolarized, and their ability to remove extracellular K+ is impaired (Djukic et al., 2007), consistent with their high expression of this channel.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Deletion of gap junction proteins that link astrocytes and oligodendrocytes produces myelin pathology comparable to what occurs in Kcnj10−/− mice.
source: In support of this hypothesis, deletion of gap junction proteins that link astrocytes and oligodendrocytes produces myelin pathology comparable to what occurs in Kcnj10−/− mice (Magnotti et al., 2011; Menichella et al., 2003), and heterozygote analysis indicates that there is a close genetic interaction between these connexin genes and Kir4.1 in producing myelin vacuolization (Menichella et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: There is a close genetic interaction between connexin genes and Kir4.1 in producing myelin vacuolization.
source: In support of this hypothesis, deletion of gap junction proteins that link astrocytes and oligodendrocytes produces myelin pathology comparable to what occurs in Kcnj10−/− mice (Magnotti et al., 2011; Menichella et al., 2003), and heterozygote analysis indicates that there is a close genetic interaction between these connexin genes and Kir4.1 in producing myelin vacuolization (Menichella et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The structure and function of oligodendrocytes is critically dependent on astrocytes.
source: Our results emphasize that both the structure and function of oligodendrocytes is critically dependent on astrocytes, and that reactive changes in astrocytes associated with reduced Kir4.1 expression (Hinterkeuser et al., 2000; Kaiser et al., 2006; MacFarlane and Sontheimer, 1997; Pivonkova et al., 2010; Tong et al., 2014) may in turn precipitate pathological changes in myelin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Membrane potential fluctuates predictably during the cell cycle in many cell types.
source: Membrane potential fluctuates predictably during the cell cycle in many cell types (Blackiston et al., 2009; Sundelacruz et al., 2009), and previous studies indicate that K+ channels play an important role in regulating cell cycle progression in OPCs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: K+ channels play an important role in regulating cell cycle progression in OPCs.
source: Membrane potential fluctuates predictably during the cell cycle in many cell types (Blackiston et al., 2009; Sundelacruz et al., 2009), and previous studies indicate that K+ channels play an important role in regulating cell cycle progression in OPCs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of delayed rectifier K+ channels in cultured OPC-like O-2A cells and OPCs in cerebellar slice cultures inhibits their proliferation and differentiation by inducing G1 arrest.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of delayed rectifier K+ channels in cultured OPC-like O-2A cells and OPCs in cerebellar slice cultures inhibits their proliferation and differentiation by inducing G1 arrest (Gallo et al., 1996; Ghiani et al., 1999; Knutson et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: OPCs upregulate Kv1.3 during G1 phase of the cell cycle, and blockade of this channel prevents G1/S transition.
source: Subsequent studies showed that OPCs upregulate Kv1.3 during G1 phase of the cell cycle, and blockade of this channel prevents G1/S transition (Chittajallu et al., 2002; Tegla et al., 2011), while overexpression of certain Kv1 isoforms promotes their proliferation, suggesting that OPC homeostasis is critically regulated by their membrane potential and potassium conductance.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Expression of Kir4.1 channels during astrocyte development correlates with a negative shift in RMP, cessation of cell proliferation, and increased differentiation.
source: Expression of Kir4.1 channels during astrocyte development correlates with a negative shift in RMP, cessation of cell proliferation, and increased differentiation (Bordey and Sontheimer, 1997; MacFarlane and Sontheimer, 2000), and astrocytes that become proliferative after injury have lower Kir current density than non-proliferating astrocytes near the injury site (MacFarlane and Sontheimer, 1997).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Heterologous expression of Kir4.1 in glioma cells induces hyperpolarization and G1 arrest.
source: In addition, heterologous expression of Kir4.1 in glioma cells induces hyperpolarization and G1 arrest, an effect nullified if cells are treated with BaCl2 to block Kir4.1 or artificially depolarized by high K+ (Higashimori and Sontheimer, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Complete removal of Kir4.1 from the CNS profoundly reduced OPC proliferation by the third postnatal week.
source: However, our studies also indicate that OPCs are profoundly influenced by their environment, as complete removal of Kir4.1 from the CNS profoundly reduced their proliferation by the third postnatal week (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on quantification of Ki67 immunostaining shown in Figure 1K.

claim: OPCs receive synaptic input from neurons.
source: OPCs receive synaptic input from neurons (Bergles et al., 2000), and the strength of these inputs is likely to be altered by changes in OPC membrane potential and membrane resistance.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: OPCs are able to regulate glutamatergic neurotransmission by shedding of cleaved NG2 ectodomains.
source: It has been shown that OPCs are able to regulate glutamatergic neurotransmission by shedding of cleaved NG2 ectodomains (Sakry et al., 2014), so even subtle alterations in OPC behavior have the potential to affect synaptic communication in the brain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Axonal Kv1 channels are abundant underneath the myelin sheath, particularly in juxtaparanodal regions.
source: Axonal Kv1 channels that control repolarization and limit re-excitation by distal nodes are abundant underneath the myelin sheath, particularly in juxtaparanodal regions that are isolated from nodes of Ranvier by septate/septate-like junctions (Einheber et al., 1997; Poliak et al., 2003; Rash et al., 2016; Wang et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: A single action potential can increase the local extracellular K+ concentration in unmyelinated tissue by as much as 1 mM from a resting level of 3–3.5 mM.
source: Although a single action potential can increase the local extracellular K+ concentration in unmyelinated tissue by as much as 1 mM from a resting level of 3–3.5 mM (Baylor and Nicholls, 1969; Frankenhaeuser and Hodgkin, 1956), and extracellular K+ levels can rise up to 10 mM during pathological conditions such as seizures (Moody et al., 1974), the potential for accumulation of K+ underneath myelin sheaths may be even greater due to the small peri-internodal volume and the barriers to diffusion presumed to be created by the paranodal septate junctions (Bellinger et al., 2008) (but see Hirano and Dembitzer, 1969; Hirano and Dembitzer, 1982; Rash et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Extracellular K+ levels can rise up to 10 mM during pathological conditions such as seizures.
source: Although a single action potential can increase the local extracellular K+ concentration in unmyelinated tissue by as much as 1 mM from a resting level of 3–3.5 mM (Baylor and Nicholls, 1969; Frankenhaeuser and Hodgkin, 1956), and extracellular K+ levels can rise up to 10 mM during pathological conditions such as seizures (Moody et al., 1974), the potential for accumulation of K+ underneath myelin sheaths may be even greater due to the small peri-internodal volume and the barriers to diffusion presumed to be created by the paranodal septate junctions (Bellinger et al., 2008) (but see Hirano and Dembitzer, 1969; Hirano and Dembitzer, 1982; Rash et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The Na+/K+ ATPase predominates in K+ clearance at lower activity regimes, but at higher frequencies and in situations of localized K+ release, Kir4.1 plays a more prominent role.
source: Analysis of K+ dynamics arising from neuronal activity in gray matter suggest that the Na+/K+ ATPase predominates in lower activity regimes, but at higher frequencies and in situations of localized K+ release, Kir4.1 plays a more prominent role in limiting extracellular K+ accumulation (Chever et al., 2010; Larsen et al., 2014; Sibille et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Kir4.1 is concentrated within the fine processes of astrocytes that surround synapses, as well as to astrocyte endfeet that contact blood vessels.
source: Kir4.1 is concentrated within the fine processes of astrocytes that surround synapses, as well as to astrocyte endfeet that contact blood vessels (Higashi et al., 2001), making it ideally situated to participate in K+ buffering.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes did not alter local K+ accumulation in the cortex after neuronal activity.
source: Indeed, astrocytes appear to dominate this process in gray matter, as deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes did not alter local K+ accumulation in the cortex after neuronal activity (Battefeld et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Deletion of Kir4.1 channels from oligodendrocytes slowed both their depolarization in response to repetitive stimulation and their repolarization after the stimulus train ended.
source: Our recordings in white matter revealed that deletion of Kir4.1 channels from oligodendrocytes slowed both their depolarization in response to repetitive stimulation and their repolarization after the stimulus train ended (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that these channels normally limit extracellular K+ transients induced by neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6.

claim: The membrane potential of astrocytes exhibited similarly delayed response kinetics in white matter of oKir4.1cKO mice.
source: These changes were not restricted to the protected space beneath myelin, as the membrane potential of astrocytes, which closely follow the extracellular K+ concentration (Chever et al., 2010; Meeks and Mennerick, 2007; Orkand et al., 1966), exhibited similarly delayed response kinetics in white matter (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6.

claim: Oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 is an important mediator of white matter extracellular K+ clearance.
source: These findings indicate that oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 is an important mediator of white matter extracellular K+ clearance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: oKir4.1cKO mice exhibited rare, but often fatal seizures.
source: Mice in which Kir4.1 was removed from oligodendrocytes exhibited rare, but often fatal seizures, and a dramatic reduction in PTZ-induced seizure threshold (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5.

claim: oKir4.1cKO mice exhibited a dramatic reduction in PTZ-induced seizure threshold.
source: Mice in which Kir4.1 was removed from oligodendrocytes exhibited rare, but often fatal seizures, and a dramatic reduction in PTZ-induced seizure threshold (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5.

claim: Several spontaneously arising rodent models of epilepsy were found to have altered Kir4.1 levels.
source: There is extensive evidence that Kir4.1 is a key regulator of neuronal excitability, but the involvement of oligodendrocytes in this process has not been demonstrated. Several spontaneously arising rodent models of epilepsy were found to have altered Kir4.1 levels (Harada et al., 2013; Nagao et al., 2013), and a single-nucleotide polymorphism in the Kir4.1 gene (kcnj10) was found to be responsible for differences in seizure susceptibility between C57BL6 and DBA/2 mice (Ferraro et al., 2004; Inyushin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: A single-nucleotide polymorphism in the Kir4.1 gene (kcnj10) was found to be responsible for differences in seizure susceptibility between C57BL6 and DBA/2 mice.
source: Several spontaneously arising rodent models of epilepsy were found to have altered Kir4.1 levels (Harada et al., 2013; Nagao et al., 2013), and a single-nucleotide polymorphism in the Kir4.1 gene (kcnj10) was found to be responsible for differences in seizure susceptibility between C57BL6 and DBA/2 mice (Ferraro et al., 2004; Inyushin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Polymorphisms in KCNJ10 are risk factors for epilepsy in humans.
source: In addition, polymorphisms in KCNJ10 are risk factors for epilepsy in humans (Buono et al., 2004; Dai et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2015; Lenzen et al., 2005), and seizures are a prominent component of the human disorder SeSAME/EAST syndrome, which results from loss-of-function mutations in KCNJ10 (Bockenhauer et al., 2009; Scholl et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes alone is sufficient to dramatically lower seizure threshold and induce spontaneous seizures.
source: However, our findings indicate that even in the absence of any structural changes to myelin, deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes alone is sufficient to dramatically lower seizure threshold and induce spontaneous seizures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Removal of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes does not alter the excitability of cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: However, recent studies indicate that removal of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes does not alter the excitability of cortical pyramidal neurons (Battefeld et al., 2016), perhaps due to the local abundance of astrocyte processes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 knockout mice displayed significant impairments in motor behaviors.
source: Oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 knockout mice also displayed significant impairments in motor behaviors (Figure 8), despite normal myelination and the absence of obvious neuronal pathology or neurodegeneration (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on behavioral testing shown in Figure 8.

claim: Motor impairments in oKir4.1cKO mice only became apparent during high-intensity activity.
source: These deficits only became apparent during high-intensity activity, consistent with an activity-dependent, rather than a neurodegenerative mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: No difference in conduction velocity was observed for myelinated or unmyelinated axon populations between control and oKir4.1cKO mice.
source: To assess whether axons are functionally preserved in the absence of oligodendrocyte Kir4.1, compound action potentials (CAPs) reflecting conduction along myelinated and unmyelinated axons were recorded in the corpus callosum (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B). No difference in conduction velocity was observed for myelinated or unmyelinated axon populations between control and oKir4.1cKO mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The brain and spinal cord of 10-week-old oKir4.1cKO animals exhibited grossly normal white matter with ample myelin and no apparent vacuolation.
source: In contrast to the striking white matter pathology exhibited by nKir4.1cKO mice, the brain and spinal cord of 10-week-old oKir4.1cKO animals exhibited grossly normal white matter with ample myelin and no apparent vacuolation (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: There was no change in the density of EGFP+ oligodendrocytes in oKir4.1cKO mice.
source: Moreover, there was no change in the density of EGFP+ oligodendrocytes (Figure 4G–H), indicating that oligodendrocyte survival was not impaired.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on quantification of immunostaining data shown in Figure 4G-H.

claim: Electron micrographs demonstrated a complete absence of vacuoles or aberrant myelin in oKir4.1cKO animals.
source: Electron micrographs containing cross-sections of corpus callosum from 10-week-old mice demonstrated a complete absence of vacuoles or aberrant myelin in oKir4.1cKO animals (Figure 4I–J).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on TEM data shown in Figure 4I-J.

claim: There was no difference in g-ratio across all axons between control and oKir4.1cKO mice.
source: Furthermore, the pattern of myelination, estimated by calculating g-ratios (diameter of axon/diameter of axon + myelin) (Figure 4K) revealed that there was no difference in g-ratio across all axons (Control: 0.743 ± 0.010 (n = 3 mice), oKir4.1cKO: 0.752 ± 0.001 (n = 3 mice), p=0.38) (Figure 4L), or in the relationship between axon diameter and g-ratio (Control: 0.16 ± 0.02 (n = 3 mice), oKir4.1cKO: 0.15 ± 0.01 (n = 3 mice), p=0.81) (Figure 4M).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on quantification of TEM data shown in Figure 4K-M.

claim: Swollen or degenerating axons were completely absent from corpus callosum of oKir4.1cKO mice.
source: In addition, swollen or degenerating axons were completely absent from corpus callosum of oKir4.1cKO mice (Figure 4I) and immunostaining for SMI32 (non-phosphorylated neurofilament), which is upregulated in degenerating axons (Lee et al., 2012), revealed no axonal pathology in the corpus callosum of control or oKir4.1cKO animals (n = 6 for both genotypes) (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on TEM and immunostaining data shown in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A-B.

claim: No difference in GFAP expression was observed between control and oKir4.1cKO animals.
source: Brain sections were also immunostained for GFAP, as astrocytes become reactive and upregulate GFAP in response to neuronal degeneration (Lee et al., 2012). No difference in GFAP expression was observed between control and oKir4.1cKO animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4C-D.

claim: Myelin and myelinated axons are not structurally altered as result of the selective removal of Kir4.1 channels from oligodendrocytes.
source: These findings indicate that myelin and myelinated axons are not structurally altered as result of the selective removal of Kir4.1channels from oligodendrocytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: oKir4.1cKO mice died much earlier than control littermates.
source: Although oKir4.1cKO mice did not exhibit alterations in the structure of myelin or progressive disability, these animals died much earlier than control littermates (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on survival analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Nearly all (11/12) oKir4.1cKO mice exhibited tonic-clonic seizures with full hindlimb extension after being injected with PTZ, while only 1/17 control mice exhibited this level of seizure severity.
source: Nearly all (11/12) oKir4.1cKO mice exhibited tonic-clonic seizures with full hindlimb extension after being injected with PTZ, while only 1/17 control mice exhibited this level of seizure severity (Figure 5B; Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 8/12 oKir4.1cKO mice and only 1/17 control mice experienced fatal seizures.
source: Moreover, 8/12 oKir4.1cKO mice and only 1/17 control mice experienced fatal seizures, and oKir4.1cKO mice had a faster seizure onset (Figure 5C–D), indicating that deletion of this K+ channel from oligodendrocytes enhances neuronal excitability and increases seizure susceptibility.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: oKir4.1cKO mice had a faster seizure onset than control mice.
source: Moreover, 8/12 oKir4.1cKO mice and only 1/17 control mice experienced fatal seizures, and oKir4.1cKO mice had a faster seizure onset (Figure 5C–D), indicating that deletion of this K+ channel from oligodendrocytes enhances neuronal excitability and increases seizure susceptibility.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental observations shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Deletion of Kir4.1 from oligodendrocytes enhances neuronal excitability and increases seizure susceptibility.
source: Moreover, 8/12 oKir4.1cKO mice and only 1/17 control mice experienced fatal seizures, and oKir4.1cKO mice had a faster seizure onset (Figure 5C–D), indicating that deletion of this K+ channel from oligodendrocytes enhances neuronal excitability and increases seizure susceptibility.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Extracellular K+ levels are slower to recover following neuronal stimulation in glia-specific Kir4.1 knockout mice.
source: Previous studies have shown that Kir4.1 is involved in buffering extracellular K+ in both gray and white matter (Bay and Butt, 2012; Chever et al., 2010; Haj-Yasein et al., 2011; Neusch et al., 2006; Sibille et al., 2014), as extracellular K+ levels are slower to recover following neuronal stimulation in glia-specific Kir4.1 knockout mice (Chever et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Oligodendrocytes were progressively depolarized during the stimulus train due to K+ release from active axons and gradually returned to baseline after cessation of the stimulus.
source: In accordance with previous studies (Battefeld et al., 2016; Yamazaki et al., 2007; 2014), oligodendrocytes were progressively depolarized during the stimulus train due to K+ release from active axons and gradually returned to baseline after cessation of the stimulus (Figure 6B–C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C) following the gradual decline in extracellular K+ levels (Battefeld et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6B-C, with citation support.

claim: Oligodendrocyte depolarization occurred more slowly in oKir4.1cKO mice.
source: Oligodendrocyte depolarization occurred more slowly in oKir4.1cKO mice, and the decay of membrane potential following cessation of stimulation was markedly prolonged relative to controls (Figure 6B–D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–D) (corpus callosum: 11.6 ± 1.6 s (n = 15) vs. 5.9 ± 0.7 s (n = 15), p=0.0036; alveus: 9.3 ± 0.6 s (n = 16) vs. 6.3 ± 0.4 s (n = 14), p=0.0017), which was also reflected in the area under the curve (Figure 6E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: The decay of oligodendrocyte membrane potential following cessation of stimulation was markedly prolonged in oKir4.1cKO mice relative to controls.
source: Oligodendrocyte depolarization occurred more slowly in oKir4.1cKO mice, and the decay of membrane potential following cessation of stimulation was markedly prolonged relative to controls (Figure 6B–D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–D) (corpus callosum: 11.6 ± 1.6 s (n = 15) vs. 5.9 ± 0.7 s (n = 15), p=0.0036; alveus: 9.3 ± 0.6 s (n = 16) vs. 6.3 ± 0.4 s (n = 14), p=0.0017), which was also reflected in the area under the curve (Figure 6E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: Astrocyte membrane potential follows the concentration of extracellular K+ closely, due to the high permeability of their membranes to K+.
source: To provide an independent assessment of extracellular K+ dynamics, we recorded the response of astrocytes in the corpus callosum and alveus of oKir4.1cKO mice (crossed to Slc1a2-EGFP mice to allow astrocyte visualization) (Figure 6F; Figure 6—figure supplement 1F). Astrocyte membrane potential follows the concentration of extracellular K+ closely, due to the high permeability of their membranes to K+ (Chever et al., 2010; Meeks and Mennerick, 2007; Orkand et al., 1966).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: A significant slowing of astrocyte decay following the end of the stimulus was observed in oKir4.1cKO mice, despite the presence of normal Kir4.1 expression by astrocytes.
source: However, despite the presence of normal Kir4.1 expression by astrocytes, a significant slowing of their decay following the end of the stimulus was observed in oKir4.1cKO mice, comparable to that observed in oligodendrocytes (Figure 6G–J; Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–J).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6G-J.

claim: Kir4.1 deletion from oligodendrocytes did not affect the mode (i.e. peak of the CAP) or median baseline conduction velocity of optic nerves.
source: Consistent with the behavior of axons in the corpus callosum (Figure 4D), Kir4.1 deletion from oligodendrocytes did not affect the mode (i.e. peak of the CAP) or median baseline conduction velocity of the nerves (n = 5 nerves from three mice for each genotype) (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: High-frequency stimulation of the optic nerve results in an increase in extracellular K+ levels and a decay of the CAP waveform.
source: It is established that high-frequency stimulation of the optic nerve results in an increase in extracellular K+ levels and a decay of the CAP waveform (Bay and Butt, 2012; Ransom et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: In young Kir4.1 KO optic nerves, there is a slower restoration of the extracellular K+ concentration after stimulation.
source: In young Kir4.1 KO optic nerves, there is a slower restoration of the extracellular K+ concentration after stimulation (Bay and Butt, 2012), suggesting that Kir4.1 plays an important role in K+ clearance in this tissue.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The CAP waveform in oKir4.1cKO optic nerves took significantly longer to recover after stimulation ended.
source: Although oKir4.1cKO nerves exhibited a similar reduction in peak amplitude during stimulation, the CAP waveform in these nerves took significantly longer to recover after stimulation ended (Figure 7E–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7E-F.

claim: The CAP integral and the median axon conduction latency also recovered more slowly in oKir4.1cKO mice.
source: The CAP integral, representing total activity in the nerve, and the median axon conduction latency also recovered more slowly in oKir4.1cKO mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The recovery of oKir4.1cKO CAPs was delayed when using lower frequency stimulation (20 Hz).
source: When the same experiments were repeated using lower frequency stimulation (20 Hz), the recovery of oKir4.1cKO CAPs was also delayed (Figure 7G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Oligodendrocyte-specific Kir4.1 deletion alters action potential conduction in both physiological and pathophysiological activity regimes.
source: These findings suggest that oligodendrocyte-specific Kir4.1 deletion alters action potential conduction in both physiological and pathophysiological activity regimes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: There was no difference in total locomotion or in rearing behavior of oKir4.1cKO mice in an open field chamber.
source: When placed in an open field chamber, there was no difference in total locomotion or in rearing behavior of oKir4.1cKO mice (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on behavioral testing shown in Figure 8A.

claim: oKir4.1cKO mice had significantly shorter latency to fall on an accelerating rotarod.
source: However, when challenged by placement on an accelerating rotarod, oKir4.1cKO mice had significantly shorter latency to fall (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on behavioral testing shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Control mice increased their running activity over time when given free access to a running wheel, eventually running 10–15 km per 24 hr period.
source: Moreover, when given free access to a running wheel over multiple days, control mice increased their running activity over time, eventually running 10–15 km per 24 hr period (Figure 8C), while oKir4.1cKO mice were unable to achieve the same performance level, and typically did not exceed 5 km per 24 hr.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on behavioral testing shown in Figure 8C.

claim: oKir4.1cKO mice were unable to achieve the same running performance level as control mice, and typically did not exceed 5 km per 24 hr.
source: Moreover, when given free access to a running wheel over multiple days, control mice increased their running activity over time, eventually running 10–15 km per 24 hr period (Figure 8C), while oKir4.1cKO mice were unable to achieve the same performance level, and typically did not exceed 5 km per 24 hr.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on behavioral testing shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The cumulative distance run over 7 days was significantly less in oKir4.1cKO mice than in control mice.
source: As a result, the cumulative distance run over 7 days was significantly less, as was the average speed during active running periods (Figure 8D–E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on behavioral testing shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The average speed during active running periods was significantly less in oKir4.1cKO mice than in control mice.
source: As a result, the cumulative distance run over 7 days was significantly less, as was the average speed during active running periods (Figure 8D–E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on behavioral testing shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Under physiologically relevant behavioral conditions, oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 channels play a vital role in facilitating neuronal activity.
source: These results suggest that, under physiologically relevant behavioral conditions, oligodendrocyte Kir4.1 channels play a vital role in facilitating neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Oligodendrocytes play a critical role in the mammalian CNS by forming myelin sheaths around axons that enable action potentials to be propagated rapidly with minimal energy expenditure.
source: Oligodendrocytes play a critical role in the mammalian CNS by forming myelin sheaths around axons that enable action potentials to be propagated rapidly with minimal energy expenditure.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about oligodendrocyte function.

claim: Oligodendrocytes provide metabolic support to axons in the form of lactate.
source: Although they were once assumed to be merely passive insulators, recent studies indicate that oligodendrocytes also provide metabolic support to axons in the form of lactate (Fünfschilling et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2012) and contribute to a larger glial network by coupling to astrocytes through gap junctions (Kamasawa et al., 2005; Mugnaini, 1986; Orthmann-Murphy et al., 2007; Rash et al., 1997; 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Oligodendrocytes contribute to a larger glial network by coupling to astrocytes through gap junctions.
source: Although they were once assumed to be merely passive insulators, recent studies indicate that oligodendrocytes also provide metabolic support to axons in the form of lactate (Fünfschilling et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2012) and contribute to a larger glial network by coupling to astrocytes through gap junctions (Kamasawa et al., 2005; Mugnaini, 1986; Orthmann-Murphy et al., 2007; Rash et al., 1997; 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Removal of oligodendrocytes by exposure to the oligotoxin cuprizone, or through genetic ablation in animal models, enhances neuronal excitability.
source: Removal of oligodendrocytes by exposure to the oligotoxin cuprizone, or through genetic ablation in animal models, enhances neuronal excitability (Hamada and Kole, 2015) that can lead to tremor and death (Traka et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Oligodendrocyte loss contributes to neurological disability in diseases such as multiple sclerosis.
source: Moreover, oligodendrocyte loss contributes to neurological disability in diseases such as multiple sclerosis, highlighting the importance of defining the mechanisms that control their form and function.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the role of oligodendrocytes in disease.

claim: Kir4.1 mRNA levels were >10 fold lower in oKir4.1cKO oligodendrocytes than in control oligodendrocytes.
source: Kir4.1 mRNA levels were >10 fold lower in oKir4.1cKO oligodendrocytes (n = 3) than in control oligodendrocytes (n = 3) (RQ = 0.063, 95% CI = 0.035–0.112) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), while oKir4.1cKO (n = 3) and control (n = 2) astrocytes showed no difference in Kir4.1 mRNA levels (RQ = 1.52, 95% CI = 0.32–7.10) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: oKir4.1cKO and control astrocytes showed no difference in Kir4.1 mRNA levels.
source: Kir4.1 mRNA levels were >10 fold lower in oKir4.1cKO oligodendrocytes (n = 3) than in control oligodendrocytes (n = 3) (RQ = 0.063, 95% CI = 0.035–0.112) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), while oKir4.1cKO (n = 3) and control (n = 2) astrocytes showed no difference in Kir4.1 mRNA levels (RQ = 1.52, 95% CI = 0.32–7.10) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: No significant changes in resting membrane potential or membrane resistance of EGFP+ oligodendrocytes were observed following selective deletion of Kir4.1.
source: In contrast to nKir4.1cKO mice (Figure 1), no significant changes in resting membrane potential (RMP) (Control: –70 ± 1 mV (n = 17) vs. oKir4.1cKO: –68 ± 1 mV (n = 26), p=0.25), membrane resistance (Rm) (Control: 33 ± 3 MΩ vs. oKir4.1cKO: 40 ± 4 MΩ, p=0.22), or I-V response of EGFP+ oligodendrocytes were observed following selective deletion of Kir4.1 (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Kir4.1 does not influence the membrane properties of mature oligodendrocytes.
source: These findings indicate that Kir4.1 does not influence the membrane properties of mature oligodendrocytes, indicating that other K+ conductances dominate at this stage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Application of BaCl2 increased the membrane resistance of control and oKir4.1cKO oligodendrocytes to a similar degree.
source: Application of BaCl2 increased the membrane resistance of control and oKir4.1cKO oligodendrocytes to a similar degree (ΔRmcontrol: 15.2 ± 3.2 MΩ, n = 25 vs. oKir4.1cKO: 19.9 ± 3.5 MΩ, n = 32; p=0.33) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.
